claims.text: Actively learned moment-tensor potentials can be parameterized using ab initio data.
An actively learned interatomic potential can reliably predict fusion free energies and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The machine-learned potential can capture anharmonic vibrational entropy.
The machine-learned potential can capture electron–vibration coupling effects.
The method will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method will be faster than TOR-TILD.
Fusion free energies from the method will agree with ab initio free-energy calculations to within approximately 5%.
Training on targeted solid and liquid configurations near melting will provide a potential suitable for sampling both phases.
The trained potential can be used for efficient molecular-dynamics sampling and thermodynamic integration.
Limited ab initio reference configurations can calibrate and validate faithful solid and liquid free energies and entropy contributions.
An iteratively refined machine-learning potential can approximate interatomic interactions with high accuracy.
Active learning will adaptively enrich the training set around phase boundaries and maintain fidelity in both solid and liquid phases.
The initial validation domain is elemental and binary systems at ambient pressure over approximately 0.8–1.2 times their melting temperature.
Extending the method to multicomponent high-entropy systems will require further calibration because of increased configurational complexity.
First-principles workflows are computationally demanding for multicomponent alloys.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations are accurate but computationally expensive for systems with anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling effects.
The ability of the potential to capture subtle electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic entropy in complex high-entropy systems is uncertain.
Deviation exceeding approximately 5% from AIMD benchmarks, or computational requirements comparable to or greater than TOR-TILD, would falsify the proposed cost–fidelity advantage.
